title: Why Circuits Need Memory
excerpt: Every gate-only circuit you've built so far forgets its inputs the instant they change. Here's the feedback trick that lets a circuit remember, and why it doesn't collapse into an infinite loop.
seoTitle: Combinational vs Sequential Logic: Why Circuits Remember
seoDescription: Combinational circuits forget their inputs instantly. See how feedback turns gates into memory, and why the loop settles instead of oscillating.

body.text: Combinational Logic: A Pure Function of Its Inputs

content.text: Half adders, multiplexers and majority voters all belong to the family of combinational logic. A combinational circuit computes output = f(inputs) with no dependence on time or previous inputs. Most of digital logic works this way, and circuits whose output depends on a sequence of inputs rather than a single snapshot are called sequential.
Of course, computers also need to remember information and that means we need logic gates that depend on previous inputs

This is done by wiring a gate's output back into one of its own inputs, either directly or through a neighboring gate that loops back. The output is no longer a function of the outside inputs, because previous outputs now affect the state of the gate.

body.text: Why This Doesn't Blow Up Into an Infinite Loop

content.text: A feedback loop in software that recomputes a value from itself is usually a bug. In a circuit it is not, and the reason is delay. Gates are not instant. Every gate takes a little time to pass a signal through, so a signal chasing itself around a loop does not recompute forever. It settles, because each pass around the loop changes the signal less than the last, until a pass finally changes nothing at all. After a handful of gate delays the loop reaches a value that agrees with itself, every gate's output matches what its inputs demand, and nothing moves after that. That settling is what makes the next three tutorials safe to build.
